result.summary: Pausanias tells how Megalopolis was founded by Arcadians gathering from many towns under Theban sponsorship, and lists the towns involved. He then recounts its history: wars with Sparta, tyrants Aristodemus and Lydiades, and its destruction by Cleomenes. He ends with the river Buphagus on the border with Heraea.

scenes.title: Founding of Megalopolis
scenes.summary: The Arcadians gather into Megalopolis, encouraged by Epaminondas, from many towns; some resist and are forced or flee.
scenes.stakes: Arcadians fear conquest by the Lacedaemonians; refusing towns risk forced removal, exile or death.

scenes.title: Early wars and tyrants
scenes.summary: Megalopolis is dated to 368/7 BC, survives the Sacred War era, and is ruled by Aristodemus, who beats Acrotatus, and later Lydiades.
scenes.stakes: The new city risks Spartan attack and Macedonian dominance.

scenes.title: Agis and Cleomenes attack
scenes.summary: Agis's battering-ram is broken by the North Wind; later Cleomenes captures and razes Megalopolis, and Philopoemen leads refugees to Messenia.
scenes.stakes: The city faces capture and destruction; its people risk slaughter.

scenes.title: River Buphagus
scenes.summary: The river Buphagus marks the border with Heraea and is said to be named for a hero killed by Artemis.
scenes.stakes: Buphagus is slain for attempting Artemis's chastity.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for the Spartans, used by Pausanias.
Epithet given to Aristodemus despite his tyranny.
Roman name for the Greek Persephone.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid claim that the North Wind saved Greeks at Sepiades and Megalopolis.

analysis.text: The passage shows how synoecism, gathering small towns into a large one, was used for security against a stronger neighbour.
Megalopolis was founded after Leuctra (371 BC) to check Sparta, showing Theban power; it later joined the Achaean League and suffered Cleomenes' sack in 223 BC.

fun_facts.text: Megalopolis means 'great city'; the historian Polybius, who came from it, wrote much about its later history.

language_notes.text: Refers to Roman colonies founded by Augustus and others, which were newer than Megalopolis (founded c. 370 BC) in Greece, such as Nicopolis and Patrae.
"Reduce" here means to subdue or conquer; the Argives swelled Argos by synoecism, merging neighbouring settlements into one city.
"Colonization" here means a planned settlement of the new city, not an overseas colony.
Trapezus on the Euxine (Black Sea) was a Greek colony, so the Arcadian Trapezuntines claimed kinship as people of its mother-city.
"Find the deity mild" means Pallantium enjoyed good fortune; Pausanias elsewhere says Antoninus Pius favoured it, so "deity" is the emperor's favour.
Dated by the Athenian archon and Olympiad, the usual Greek method; the 102nd Olympiad's second year corresponds to about 368/7 BC.
The Sacred War (356–346 BC): Phocis seized Delphi's treasures to fund its war against Thebes and its allies.
Chæronea (338 BC) was where Philip of Macedon defeated the Greek allies, ending Greek independence.
"Good man and True" is a nickname, ironic for a tyrant, since he held power unconstitutionally.
Refers to the storm at the Sepiades (Sepias) rocks that wrecked Persian ships in 480 BC during Xerxes' invasion.
"Rased" is an old spelling of "razed": levelled to the ground.
"Autocracy" here means sole rule by Cleomenes, who abolished the dual kingship and the ephors' power.

context_notes.text: Epaminondas of Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC and backed Arcadian unity to check Spartan power.
Demeter and Proserpine (the Greek Persephone) were the chief goddesses of Lycosura, whose sanctuary offered asylum.
The Achæan League was a federation of Peloponnesian cities; Aratus of Sicyon was its famous leader.
Philopœmen, born at Megalopolis, later became a leading general of the Achæan League; Pausanias treats him later.
Artemis was the virgin goddess of hunting, who punished those who threatened her chastity.

literary_notes.text: The Argive precedent serves as an argument by example, justifying the Arcadians' motive through an earlier success.
The long list of towns recalls Homeric catalogues, conveying the scale of the migration and giving the history a monumental weight.
Pausanias reports the violence flatly, with phrases like "fierce anger", leaving the grim cost of unification to speak for itself.
The curt remark undercuts the previous sentence's security, hinting that the Megalopolitans' confidence was mistaken.
The North Wind is treated as a purposeful benefactor of Greece, saving them twice.
Lydiades' heroic death fits his earlier portrayal as ambitious yet patriotic, closing his story.
